l: soft water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Soft water is useful for photographic processes: developers remain effective longer, and carbon printing proceeds more rapidly or at a lower temperature. Rain-water collected in a town or densely populated district and flowing over dirty roofs may contain carbonaceous and organic constituents, limiting use.

l: automatic shunt for diverting rainwater, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: An automatic shunt for diverting rain-water prevents water from entering a cistern until roofs have been thoroughly washed, then provides clean, serviceable soft water. It uses valve V, lever L, weight W, and can C with a small hole; a movable strainer protects the cataract hole. Its operation requires adjustment of the weight and valve opening angle, and the can restores the apparatus after rain ceases.

l: BLACK PHOSPHORUS, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: P. Thenard describes black phosphorus as perhaps not invariably a mixture of ordinary phosphorus and metallic phosphide traces. A specimen melted white, stayed white after cooling, then turned black after superfusion and contact with white or black phosphorus; it largely dissolved in carbon disulphide.

l: P. THENARD, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: contends the customary mixture explanation is not admissible in all cases BLACK PHOSPHORUS.] P. Thenard challenges the customary explanation of black phosphorus as a mixture of ordinary phosphorus with traces of a metallic phosphide. He submitted a specimen of black or dark gray phosphorus to the Academy and reported its changes under melting, cooling, superfusion, and contact with other forms of phosphorus.

l: steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Steep water is water in which malt has been steeped. It contains 1.08 percent total dry matter: 0.56 percent organic matter and 0.52 percent mineral matter, plus 0.033 percent nitrogen. Its mineral matter includes potash, phosphoric acid, lime, soda, magnesia, sulphuric acid, and traces of oxide of iron, with no chlorine or silica.

l: composition of steep water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The composition of steep water includes 0.193 percent potash, 0.031 percent phosphoric acid, 0.012 percent lime, 0.047 percent soda, 0.016 percent magnesia, and 0.007 percent sulphuric acid. Oxide of iron is present in traces, while chlorine and silica are absent.

l: Schreiber's apparatus for revivifying bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Schreiber's apparatus continuously revivifies used bone-black, transferring it from wells through washing, filtering, drying, furnace retorts, and cooling, with automatic elevator and gearing operation.

l: bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Bone-black loses decolorizing power as sugar-refining salts and insoluble compounds fill its pores; Schreiber's apparatus washes, elevates, dries, heats, cools, and discharges it for bagging and reuse.

l: revivification of bone-black, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Revivification of bone-black restores it for reuse by freeing it from absorbed salts and insoluble compounds, unfolding from formerly employed fermentation toward washing with water and acid in a rotary washer.

l: rotary washer, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Rotary washer receives bone-black directly from wells and discharges it near a steam filter beneath the floor, which sends wet black toward an elevator and drier.

l: automatic drying system, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The automatic drying system, located at the upper part of the animal black furnace, dries bone-black as it exits the washer. It consists of two undulating pipes with steam openings; waste heat and combustion products pass between them and leave through the chimney.

l: animal black furnace, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The animal black furnace is Schreiber's apparatus for continuously revivifying bone-black. It has a masonry casing, coke-fired fire-place chamber, automatic upper drying system, and retorts in two rows. Bone-black moves from hopper through drier and retorts to cooling pipes and rotary cylinders, which regulate discharge into a rail car. It revivifies 120 hectoliters daily using 360–400 kilogrammes of coke.

l: soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.] The article presents practical instructions for consumers to make pure and unadulterated soap. It explains that soap made with tallow or grease can be nearly as hard as soda soap, while soap made with oil can be remelted with water to produce a bright, harder, and stiffer product.

l: consumers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.] Consumers are shown how to make neutral potash soap for household and laundry use. The article cautions them to distinguish genuine caustic potash from products falsely sold as potash.

l: potash soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Potash soap is a soap described as superior to soda soap, especially for washing wool or woolen fabrics. Made with pure, neutral caustic potash, it suits wool washing, household use, and laundry. It may be made from tallow, grease, vegetable or animal oil, or cotton seed oil; the latter lathers very freely. It can be hardened by remelting with water and is made by fleece scouring.

l: soda soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Soda soap is a soap considered inferior to potash soap, especially for washing wool or woolen fabrics, even when pure and well made.

l: caustic soda, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Caustic soda is a caustic alkali in powdered 98 per cent form, distinct from caustic potash despite similar appearance, and sold by lye packers as crystal, ball, or rock potash, often adulterated.

l: hard soap, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_made_with caustic soda [using pure powdered caustic soda] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.] The method for making pure neutral potash soap is said to be almost identical to the method for making hard soap with pure powdered caustic soda. Potash soap made with tallow can become nearly as hard as soda soap.

l: wool and woolen fabrics, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_washed_with potash soap [with advantages over soda soap] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.] Potash soap is recommended for washing wool and woolen fabrics because it is considered superior to soda soap for this purpose. The article says it can be used to wash wool and the cloth made from it.

l: tallow or grease, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_used_for potash soap [by farmers and householders as the cheapest readily available material] SOAP AND ITS MANUFACTURE, FROM A CONSUMER'S POINT OF VIEW.] Tallow or grease should be free from salt before being used to make potash soap. Eighty pounds are melted, cooled to about 130 F, and mixed with caustic potash lye; the article identifies these materials as economical and readily available to farmers and householders.

l: cotton seed oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Cotton seed oil is an oil valued chiefly for soap, plaster, and Pharmacopoeia preparations. It is recommended for manufacturers and laundry soap because it produces a magnificent, freely lathering soap. With one and one-half pints of boiling water under the U. S. P. process, it produces lead plaster as good as olive-oil plaster and can substitute for olive oil. It makes better-consistency Linimentum Ammoniae, is superior to olive oil in Linimentum Camphorae because it dissolves camphor much better, and performs well in Linimentum Chloroformi. It is not adapted to Linimentum Calcis: it does not readily saponify and separates quickly. It is very soluble in chloroform. Mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it becomes reddish in twelve to twenty-four hours, allowing detection in olive oil at five percent or less.

l: fleece scouring, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Fleece scouring is a wool washing practice: wool is washed while growing on sheep with potash soap made from waste tallow, improving wool for marketing and cleaning sheep skin for sheep owners.

l: S.S. Bradford, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: S.S. Bradford, a Ph.G., manufactured lead plaster for six years and investigated cotton seed oil as an olive-oil substitute in liniments.

l: lead plaster, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_quality equally as good as plaster made with olive oil [when made with cotton seed oil under the stated process] Lead plaster made with cotton seed oil was found by S.S. Bradford to be equally as good as that made with olive oil when the U. S. P. process was modified by using one and one-half pints of boiling water instead of one-half pint.

l: olive oil, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: does_not_assume_color_change reddish [when pure and mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis] Olive oil was the oil traditionally used by S.S. Bradford for lead plaster and was compared with cotton seed oil in several liniments. When pure olive oil is mixed with liquor plumbi subacetatis, it does not undergo the reddish color change observed with cotton seed oil.

l: Prof. de Chaumont, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: delivered lecture on food and energy [at the Sanitary Congress in Newcastle-on-Tyne] Prof. de Chaumont delivered a lecture at the Sanitary Congress at Newcastle-on-Tyne on September 28, 1882. He discussed the uses and classes of food, the energy of the body, alcohol, fatigue, tobacco, and scurvy among seamen.

l: man, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Man is probably naturally a fruit-eating animal resembling monkeys, but began consuming animal food long ago; his digestive apparatus can digest any useful nourishment, and his system accommodates dietary change.

l: food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Food is any substance taken into the body to build or repair tissues, provide energy and animal heat, or control or assist these functions. Broadly, it includes water and air, though they are not ordinarily recognized as food.

l: human nutrition, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Human nutrition requires food, nitrogenous substances for tissue building, repair, and renewal, and irreplaceable salts. It is best maintained through a due admixture and variety of four alimentary classes, with water and salts; dietary monotony can seriously impair health, digestion, and assimilation.

l: energy of the body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: derives_from non-nitrogenous food [especially fats, starches, and sugars] The energy of the body is derived from food, particularly from its non-nitrogenous parts. Heat is described as a form of convertible energy that can perform useful or productive work.

l: organic substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Organic substances are divided into nitrogen-containing substances and substances that do not contain nitrogen. The latter include fats, starches, and sugars.

l: nitrogenous substances, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Nitrogenous substances contain nitrogen and are needed to build tissues in the young and repair and renew them in adults; they include animal and vegetable forms, then contribute to bodily energy when broken down and oxidized.

l: non-nitrogenous food, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Non-nitrogenous food includes fats, starches, and sugars, which modern experiments say provide most bodily energy.

l: fats, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: contain no nitrogen [as organic constituents] Fats are non-nitrogenous constituents that contribute energy. Examples recommended in a varied diet include butter, lard, suet, and oil.

l: starches and sugars, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: contain no nitrogen [as organic constituents] Starches and sugars are non-nitrogenous food constituents that provide energy. Examples include starch from wheat, potatoes, rice, and peas, as well as cane-sugar and milk-sugar.

l: human body, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a machine [in relation to its work and food requirements] The human body is compared to a machine or engine that requires fuel in proportion to the work performed and the speed at which it is done. Its tissues and fluids, except fat, contain nitrogen, and its processes follow universal physical laws.

l: alcohol, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Alcohol may be a comfort and blessing when properly used, but excess makes it a bane and curse. Up to about one and a half to two pints of beer it provides convertible energy; beyond that, considerable doses give temporary stimulus followed by depression and are generally avoided before or during work.

l: scurvy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Scurvy is a serious maritime health problem of vital importance to a maritime nation, associated with inadequate or monotonous provisions; it may result when lime-juice regulations are neglected, and prevention requires varied food, proper lime-juice, and potatoes.

l: scientific experiments on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Scientific experiments and the work of Joule, Lyon Playfair, Clausius, Tyndall, Helmholtz, and others established that heat is a mode of motion and convertible energy. Experiments by Dr. Parkes at the laboratory at Netley showed that alcohol beyond a limited amount did not provide convertible energy.

l: scurvy outbreaks, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Scurvy outbreaks, possibly linked to neglected varied food scales and lime-juice regulations, increased again to ninety-nine in 1881 after seriously falling since 1873.

l: lecture on food and energy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A lecture at the Sanitary Congress in Newcastle-on-Tyne examines food classification, nutrition and bodily work, dietary variety, alcohol and tobacco, scurvy among seamen, and protection of maritime health.

l: Henry H. Croft, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Henry H. Croft, an author at Hermanitas Ranch, reports Texas experiments on rattlesnake poison, testing iodine and questioning potassium permanganate after absorption.

l: Mr. Pedler, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: shows rattlesnake poison [that it is destroyed or neutralized by platinic chloride] Mr. Pedler reported that snake poison is destroyed or neutralized by platinic chloride, probably through formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride. He also referred to potassium permanganate but allowed that it would probably be ineffective after the poison had been absorbed.

l: Texas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Texas is a place where rattlesnakes commonly endanger campers, where Croft observed poison at Hermanitas Ranch, and where farms rose from 61,125 in 1870 to 174,184.

l: rattlesnake poison, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Rattlesnake poison is a poisonous principle associated with snakes, suggested to be an alkaloid-like substance. From a fully charged gland it appears white and opaque; with iodine it forms an insoluble iodo compound and dense light-brown amorphous precipitate.

l: rattlesnake, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Croft killed a moderately sized rattlesnake identified as Crotalus horridus that had not bitten anything. Its poison gland was fully charged with white, opaque poison, and its bladder contained a considerable quantity of light-brown amorphous ammonium urate.

l: rattlesnake bites, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_treated_with iodine solution [applied as soon as possible to the wound] Croft says iodine in potassium iodide is a favored remedy for rattlesnake bites in Texas. He reports having observed the mixture's efficacy in two cases, one involving a buck and the other a dog.

l: iodine, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: forms iodo compound [an insoluble compound with rattlesnake poison, if the poison is an alkaloid] Iodine was proposed as a possible antidotal agent because it formed a precipitate with rattlesnake poison, as it does with many alkaloids. Croft observed a dense light-brown precipitate immediately after adding iodine solution to the poison.

l: potassium iodide, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A strong solution of iodine in potassium iodide is described as a popular Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites. Potassium iodide can also be combined with ferric chloride to make an extemporaneous solution for testing alkaloids and perhaps snake poison.

l: iodine solution, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Iodine solution, a favorite Texas remedy for rattlesnake bites, contains iodine in potassium iodide and, when tested on rattlesnake poison, immediately formed a dense light-brown noncrystalline precipitate.

l: platinic chloride, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: destroys_or_neutralizes rattlesnake poison [probably by forming an insoluble double platinic chloride] Platinic chloride was reported by Mr. Pedler to destroy or neutralize snake poison. Croft attributes this action probably to formation of an insoluble double platinic chloride, as occurs with almost all alkaloids.

l: alkaloids, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The poisonous principle in snakes was described by a French chemist as possibly belonging to the alkaloids. Croft compared the reaction of rattlesnake poison with iodine to the precipitates produced by most alkaloids and mentions a ferric chloride and potassium iodide mixture as a convenient alkaloid test.

l: The Chinese Sign Manual, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Chinese Sign Manual concerns the use of finger, thumb, and palm impressions as signatures in China. It describes their application in courts, the army, and transactions involving the sale or divorce of persons.

l: Henry Faulds, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Henry Faulds, affiliated with Tzukiyi Hospital, studies Japanese fingertip skin-furrows, links them to heredity and ethnic bearing, and seeks Chinese information.

l: W. J. Herschel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: W. J. Herschel, a government agent, administers Indian registration offices for twenty years, uses finger marks to prevent personation and repudiation, and seeks information on hand skin-furrows.

l: England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: England is described as serious rather than lucid: its thinkers retreated from free inquiry when it conflicted with established beliefs and conventions, and lucidity remained unfounded.

l: India, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: India contains troops; for twenty years, W. J. Herschel used finger marks in registration offices against personation and repudiation; later soldiers might benefit from the apparatus.

l: Egypt, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a_location_for soldier [where the apparatus could be used in the field] The apparatus was described as potentially useful to soldiers serving in Egypt, particularly for obtaining good water and cooking food in the field.

l: skin-furrows on the hand, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Skin-furrows on the hand are examined as a subject for sign manuals, medical jurisprudence, and ethnology, inviting information from Henry Faulds and W. J. Herschel.

l: medical jurisprudence, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Medical jurisprudence is identified as one field to which the study of skin-furrows may have a bearing. The unit particularly connects digital signatures with the legal validation of confessions.

l: ethnology, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Ethnology is identified as another field potentially affected by the study of skin-furrows. The text concludes that finger rugae do not provide a reliable basis for distinguishing populations.

l: heredity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Heredity is connected with Henry Faulds's observations on the finger-tips of the Japanese. The unit concludes that finger striae are not a basis for studying heredity.

l: fingerprint identification, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Fingerprint identification uses finger, thumb, and palm impressions as sign manuals or document attestations. Because finger rugae remain stable from cradle to grave, these marks resist personation and repudiation, including when a person cannot write in sales of children or women.

l: Chinese courts, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Chinese courts require thumb-print signatures on confessions, using women’s right thumbs and men’s left; without the prisoner’s print, a confession is not legally valid for execution.

l: the army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: uses fingerprint identification [to prevent personation] The army sometimes requires digital signatures to prevent personation. The general in command at Wenchow enforces the practice among his troops, and descriptions of persons note the relative numbers of volutes and coniferous finger-tips.

l: criminals, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Criminals in Chinese courts must attest their confessions with thumb-prints before they can legally be executed. A contumacious culprit may be tortured until he performs this required act.

l: confession, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A confession requires a prisoner's thumb-print attestation to be valid, enabling the legal execution of a criminal in Chinese courts.

l: personation and repudiation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Personation and repudiation are the acts that finger marks are used to prevent in Indian registration offices and in military applications. The text also describes digital signatures as difficult to forge or repudiate.

l: Chinese people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Chinese people are described as having finger rugae differing from Europeans’, but the variation lacks enough uniformity to support ethnic distinction or heredity.

l: Europeans, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: differ_from Chinese people [in finger rugae] Europeans are used as a comparison group for Chinese finger rugae. The text states that Chinese and European rugae differ, but that the observed variation does not support reliable ethnic classification.

l: Matthew Arnold, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Matthew Arnold, speaking at Liverpool University College and School of Medicine’s reopening, urges schools and universities to cultivate lucidity, which he calls England’s great want.

l: lucidity, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Lucidity is a quality and a French national turn: perceiving that long-current notions lack truth and validity and can no longer serve, an inevitable, indispensable condition for serious intellectual and spiritual construction of the future.

l: French people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: possess lucidity [as a national disposition] The French people are described as having a national turn for lucidity. They are also said to display, alongside lucidity, a want of seriousness and reverence.

l: English people, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: possess seriousness [as a national quality] The English people are described as naturally serious and as possessing reverence, respect, and love for the past. Arnold suggested that lucidity, when it came among them, might be joined to these qualities without the dangers seen elsewhere.

l: seriousness, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_valuable quality [despite accompanying defects] Seriousness is presented as a valuable and indispensable quality of England, even though it may be accompanied by false ideas, prejudice, and other disagreeable defects. Arnold contrasts it with the French tendency toward lucidity.

l: Voltaire, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Voltaire is presented as France’s principal eighteenth-century agent of lucidity, opposing absurdity and benefiting cultivated classes through that quality, though he harmed France through want of seriousness and reverence rather than lucidity.

l: Luther, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_antipathy_to immorality Luther is admired for working for conduct, which Arnold says was more than working merely for intelligence. Like Voltaire, Luther opposed the object of his antipathy with conviction, energy, genius, and masterly power, carrying his world with him.

l: Salvation Army, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Salvation Army is a movement marked by numbers, funds, energy, devotedness, excitement, and conversions, yet lacks lucidity because its assumed foundation is no longer possible or receivable.

l: Dr. Pusey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: had pure life [long-devoted, laborious, influential, and pathetic] Dr. Pusey is described as having recently ended a long, devoted, laborious, influential, pure, and pathetic life. The movement associated with his earlier name is said to have produced people worthy of respect, admiration, and love, but also to have rested on assumptions that lucidity would have exposed as unsound.

l: schools and universities, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_best_agency_for_generating lucidity [through serious and disinterested studies continued into manhood] Schools and universities are presented as the best agency for generating lucidity, especially through serious and disinterested studies connected with one another and continued into adult life. Arnold says that this process may be slow but is sure.

l: apparatus for entering flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A protective envelope for entering flames, designed to let a person enter without being burned. It unfolds as metallic-gauze armor, helmet, cuirass, skirt, boots, and shield, worn over coarse cloth soaked in alum solution, with asbestos cloth covering head, hands, and feet.

l: Humphry Davy, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: discovered metallic gauze [its cooling effect on flames] Humphry Davy observed that very fine wire gauze cooled a flame so that it could not pass through the meshes. He attributed the effect to the metal's conductivity and radiating power and used it in constructing a miners' lamp.

l: Chevalier Aldini, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Chevalier Aldini, from Milan, applied Davy’s wire-gauze discovery to an apparatus allowing a person to enter flames, then traveled across Europe giving free demonstrations, including before Paris’s Academic des Sciences committee.

l: metallic gauze, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Metallic gauze cooled flames enough to prevent them from traversing its meshes. In Aldini's apparatus it formed the protective armor, double-gauze boots, and a shield, and it was also used to cover a basket carrying a child.

l: asbestos cloth, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Asbestos cloth covered the wearer's head, hands, and feet beneath or within the metallic-gauze apparatus. A single layer was used for the bonnet and stockings, while double layers formed the gloves, and a child carried into flames wore an asbestos bonnet.

l: Aldini's demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: In Paris, before the Academic des Sciences, Aldini's demonstrations showed protective apparatus: a finger wrapped in asbestos and double wire gauze endured flame, while assistants handled hot iron, carried firebrands, and entered intense flames.

l: Paris, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: In Paris, an exhibition was held before a committee from the Academic des Sciences. Two burning straw fences formed a passage through which six men wearing Aldini suits walked, while one carried an eight-year-old child in a wire-gauze-covered basket.

l: Aldini's six experimenters, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Aldini's six experimenters demonstrate apparatus for entering flames in Paris: wearing Aldini suits, they repeatedly walk between fed blazing straw fences, while one carries an eight-year-old child protected only by an asbestos bonnet.

l: fire-walking demonstrations, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: use apparatus for entering flames [to protect experimenters from fire] In some demonstrations, experimenters holding firebrands walked for five minutes over a large grating beneath which fagots were burning. Aldini's six experimenters also walked through a narrow passage between blazing fences, and one man later entered a clear fire whose flames rose eighteen feet while carrying a child.

l: hot-house experiments, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Hot-house experiments tested human resistance to extreme heat: Banks, Blagden, and Solander spent ten minutes at 211°F with near-normal body temperatures; Blagden later lasted eight minutes at 262°F, where eggs baked hard in twenty minutes.

l: human resistance to heat, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Human resistance to heat is greater in dry than vapor-saturated air, aided by perspiration evaporating to cool the body. As external heat rises, reduced carbonic-acid exhalation and internal combustion partly support it; moving dry air is tolerable, but hot liquids or solids are especially dangerous.

l: human respiration in flames, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Human respiration in flames is presented as possible in experiments using apparatus for entering flames; it depends chiefly on human organs’ resistance to heat, not exclusively on wire-gauze cooling of inhaled air.

l: Egyptian mysteries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Egyptian mysteries are initiation rites described by Abbe Terrason in Sethos, possibly involving a fire-traversal trial. The account considers crossing a burning chamber on a grate above a ditch fire, allowing passage without flames reaching the initiate.

l: building stone supply, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_historical_status limited use before the nineteenth century [in the United States] The building stone supply developed slowly in the United States because early settlers relied mainly on wood and imported brick and stone. The unit traces the growth of domestic quarrying and describes the principal American sources and uses of granite, freestone, limestone, marble, slate, and other stones.

l: stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a building material Stone was used only slightly as a building material in the early history of the country. Loose stone was readily gathered for foundations, while more substantial building stone was initially imported by Dutch and English settlers.

l: Boston, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: uses foreign products [brick, tile, slate, and stone for described buildings] Boston used imported brick, tile, slate, and stone in its early buildings. King's Chapel in Boston was identified as the first recorded building constructed from American stone.

l: King's Chapel, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: King's Chapel, a Boston building erected in 1752, was the first recorded building made from American granite from Braintree, Mass.

l: granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Granite is a rock, particularly abundant in New England and found in lesser quantities elsewhere; with little grain, it can be quarried into blocks for buildings, monuments, paving, and breakwaters.

l: New England, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: New England contains especially abundant granite and also has sandstone, marble, and slate sources. Granite from the region became an important building material, while much of its marble was described as inferior to that of Vermont and Berkshire, Massachusetts.

l: Quincy granite, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Quincy granite, weighing about 165 pounds per cubic foot, was shipped to distant markets and used in the old Merchants' Exchange, Astor House, the Custom House in New Orleans, and many Atlantic coast buildings.

l: Quincy quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Quincy quarries, among the first extensively developed granite quarries in the United States, began work early in the nineteenth century, produced Quincy granite for distant markets, and in 1827 connected to the Neponset River by a three-mile horse railroad.

l: Quincy, Mass., Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Quincy, Massachusetts, became an important center of granite production early in the nineteenth century. Its granite was transported to distant markets, including New Orleans, and was used in numerous prominent buildings.

l: New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: New York gained 25,000 farms, 11.5 percent since 1870, while its early major buildings used Quincy granite, marble, Staten Island granite, and sandstone from Portland and other quarrying regions.

l: Georgia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 138,626 [up from 69,956 since 1870] Georgia's number of farms increased from 69,956 to 138,626, or nearly 100 percent.

l: freestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a sandstone [an earlier-used building material than granite] Freestone, or sandstone, came into use earlier than granite, although its American use was still relatively late. It was used for buildings, paving, curbing, sidewalks, and furnace hearth-stones.

l: Portland quarries, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Portland quarries, sandstone quarries opposite Middletown on the Connecticut River, were worked before the Revolution, shipped stone widely, and became associated with fossil bird footprints discovered in 1802.

l: Portland stone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_used_in brownstone fronts [mostly in New York City] Portland stone supplied most of the brownstone fronts in New York City, although some buildings used thin layers of it over brick walls. It was widely distributed from the Portland quarries.

l: Ohio, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Ohio produces light gray sandstone and undergoes an industrial revolution as its farms increase 26.1 percent in ten years.

l: limestone, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Limestone is a building and road material, used where granite or sandstone is not readily available and sometimes hammer-dressed to resemble granite. It is especially suited to macadamizing roads and sidewalks. Quarried on the premises, it is burned in a kiln into lime for building; heat expansion requires the kiln well to contract toward the top for drawing out lime.

l: Florida, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 23,438 [against 10,241 in 1870] Florida reported 23,438 farms, compared with 10,241 in 1870.

l: marble, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Marble is a stone closely related to limestone, abundant in the United States in many colors and varieties. Used for statuary, gravestones, ornament, and increasingly building exteriors, it came notably from Vermont and eastern and southern belts and was exported to Cuba.

l: Girard College, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_built_of marble [among the earliest marble buildings] Girard College was among the earliest marble buildings mentioned in the unit. Its pillars came from Berkshire, Massachusetts, which ranked next after Vermont in marble reputation.

l: Rutland, Vt., Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: produces marble [the finest American marble; fit for statuary] Rutland, Vermont, was identified as the source of American marble fully as fine as famous Carrara marble. The surrounding belt yielded the largest variety and choicest specimens, including the only quality described as fit for statuary.

l: slate, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Slate, once imported mainly from Wales for colonial gravestones, roofing, and schools, became increasingly quarried in America during the nineteenth century, reaching an annual capacity of 20,000 cases valued at $10 each by 1860.

l: North Carolina, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 78 per cent [since 1870] North Carolina's number of farms increased 78 percent since 1870.

l: Industrial Revolution, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a industrial change The division and multiplication of farms in several Southern States, together with broader changes in agricultural organization, are described as an industrial revolution.

l: Census, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: gives_account_of increase in the number of farms [as its most interesting change] The Census gives account of a near doubling in the number of farms within twenty years and provides state-level comparisons of farm growth.

l: farms, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Farms nearly doubled within twenty years, increasing even in older Northern States through estate division, new settlement, and city-and-town demand favoring moderate-sized farms for agricultural products.

l: farm owners or occupants, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Farm owners or occupants, who own or rent and cultivate farms, increased by 205,000 in six states over a decade and stood differently from wage laborers.

l: great estates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_divided_into farms [in large part of the increase] The division of great estates contributed substantially to the increase in the number of farms.

l: population of the country, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_growth_rate less than the growth rate of farms [within twenty years] The population of the country did not increase in the same proportion as the number of farms.

l: United States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The country experienced a major increase in the number of farms, with especially rapid growth in newer western and several Southern regions. The exhibition is intended to support instruction about materials used for food and clothing, as well as the study and cultivation of American trees.

l: cities and towns, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: create markets [through growth] The growth of cities and towns created markets for larger supplies of products that could be advantageously grown on moderate-sized farms.

l: agriculture, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Agriculture changed through the multiplication and division of farms. Southern agriculture generally continued to favor large farms and the employment of many hands where land remained abundant.

l: division of estates, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Division of estates drives farm growth, especially in older Southern States, and foreshadows political changes there.

l: Northern States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The number of farms increased even in the older Northern States, though less than in the far West and South. Growth became greater in Northern States farther west toward the Mississippi River.

l: Southern States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: have_tendency_toward large farms [with employment of many hands] Several Southern States experienced very large increases in farms. In some regions the growth resulted mainly from new settlements, while in several older Southern States it reflected the division of estates.

l: New Jersey, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 12.2 per cent [since 1870] New Jersey's number of farms increased 12.2 percent.

l: Pennsylvania, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 22.7 per cent [since 1870] Pennsylvania's number of farms increased 22.7 percent.

l: Indiana, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 20.3 per cent [in ten years] Indiana's number of farms increased 20.3 percent in ten years.

l: Illinois, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 26.1 per cent [in ten years] Illinois's number of farms increased 26.1 percent in ten years.

l: Michigan, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase over 55 per cent [after new railroads opened new regions] Michigan experienced an increase of more than 55 percent in the number of farms, as new railroads opened regions to settlement.

l: Wisconsin, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 28 per cent [with railroad-mileage increase about the same as Michigan] Wisconsin had about the same increase in railroad mileage as Michigan but reported only a 28 percent increase in farms.

l: Iowa, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 60 per cent Iowa's number of farms increased by 60 percent.

l: Minnesota, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase nearly 100 per cent Minnesota's number of farms increased by nearly 100 percent.

l: Kansas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 138,561 [against 38,202 in 1870] Kansas reported 138,561 farms, compared with 38,202 in 1870.

l: Nebraska, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 63,387 [against 12,301 in 1870] Nebraska reported 63,387 farms, compared with 12,301 in 1870.

l: Dakota, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 17,435 [against 1,720 in 1870] Dakota reported 17,435 farms, compared with 1,720 in 1870.

l: Northwest, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Northwest experienced especially rapid farm growth through the settlement of new land and the creation of new States.

l: new States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: undergo creation [rather than social and industrial change] In the newer regions, the increase in farms represented the creation of new States more than a change in the existing social and industrial condition of the population.

l: Arkansas, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 94,433 [against 49,424 in 1870] Arkansas reported 94,433 farms, compared with 49,424 in 1870.

l: Missouri, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 215,575 [against 148,228 in 1870] Missouri reported 215,575 farms, compared with 148,228 in 1870.

l: Virginia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 44,668 [60.5 per cent within the past ten years] Virginia had about 77,000 farms thirty years earlier and gained 44,668 farms, or 60.5 percent, within the past ten years.

l: West Virginia, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase nearly 60 per cent [over the preceding decade] West Virginia had few more farms than New Jersey ten years earlier but later had nearly twice as many and gained nearly 60 percent.

l: South Carolina, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 80 per cent [since 1870] South Carolina's number of farms increased 80 percent since 1870.

l: Alabama, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_number_of_farms 135,864 [up from 67,382 since 1870] Alabama reported 135,864 farms, compared with 67,382 in 1870, an increase of more than 100 percent.

l: Kentucky, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 40 per cent [from 118,422 to 166,453 farms] Kentucky's number of farms increased from 118,422 to 166,453, or 40 percent.

l: Tennessee, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 40 per cent [from 118,141 to 165,650 farms] Tennessee's number of farms increased from 118,141 to 165,650, or 40 percent.

l: Mississippi, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase less than 50 per cent [from 68,023 to 101,772 farms] Mississippi's number of farms increased from 68,023 to 101,772, or less than 50 percent.

l: Louisiana, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_farm_increase 70 per cent [from 28,481 to 48,292 farms] Louisiana's number of farms increased from 28,481 to 48,292, or 70 percent.

l: railroads, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: New railroads opened new regions to settlement, notably in Michigan. Similar increases in railroad mileage did not produce the same farm growth in Wisconsin.

l: settlement of new land, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The settlement of new land was a major cause of farm growth in the far Northwest and in several Southern States.

l: six older Southern States, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Six Southern States, Alabama, West Virginia, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia, had strongest estate division, with 310,795 more farm owners than ten years earlier.

l: political changes, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_expected within a few years [as a result of the industrial revolution in six older Southern States] The increase in farm owners or occupants in the six older Southern States is expected to bring important political changes within a few years.

l: A FARMER'S LIME KILN, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A FARMER'S LIME KILN is a limestone structure for burning lime, built at the foot of a steep bluff from stone quarried on the spot. It is 13 feet square and 25 feet high from the foundation, reinforced with iron rods, and includes an arch and a contracted well lined one course deep with fire-brick. The well is 7 feet wide at the bilge and has a 2-foot hole for drawing lime. Filled by hand-car on a railway track from the bluff, it uses coal and produces about 100 bushels in 24 hours.

l: burning lime, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Burning lime in the kiln requires skill and judgment. The heat must be regulated because excessive heat may cause the stones to melt or run together, while insufficient heat will leave them improperly burned.

l: lime, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_produced_by A FARMER'S LIME KILN The kiln produces about 100 bushels of lime in 24 hours. The lime is drawn through a two-foot-diameter opening beneath the well, and the quantity and quality of the resulting lime depend partly on the fuel and heat used.

l: coal, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The kiln is designed for coal and requires about three-quarters of a ton of coal per 100 bushels of lime for the stone described. The amount varies with the quality of the stone and is best determined by experimentation.

l: Oswego County, New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: contains apple jelly factories (Oswego County) [five factories in operation] Oswego County, New York, had five apple jelly factories in operation according to Dewitt C. Peck. Its natural or ungrafted apple crop remained sufficient to keep the jelly factories and numerous cider mills fairly well employed despite a broader failure of the apple crop.

l: Mexico, New York, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The largest apple jelly factory was located near the village of Mexico, New York, on Salmon Creek, whose water supplied the necessary power.

l: apple jelly factories (Oswego County), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_count five [in operation] Five apple jelly factories operated in Oswego County, New York. They used enough available natural or ungrafted apples to remain fairly well employed, and such institutions provided farmers with a use for perishable fruit that otherwise had little or no market value.

l: apple jelly factory (Mexico, New York), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The apple jelly factory, largest in the county and near Mexico, New York, used Salmon Creek water power. Erected late in 1880, it had a main-floor saw mill, eight apple-storage bins, and equipment for washing, grating, pressing, defecating, evaporating, and seed recovery. About six men ordinarily produced 1,500–1,800 pounds daily; it made about forty-five tons of jelly in 1880, plus cider and boiled cider, with improvements expected to exceed a ton daily.

l: apple jelly manufacture, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: uses apples [including natural or ungrafted, crabbed, gnarled, and frozen fruit] Apple jelly manufacture at the Mexico factory begins with apples being washed by water, grated, and pressed, after which the cider is clarified in a steam-heated defecator and concentrated in an evaporator. The process uses water power for the press and other machinery, steam at about twenty-five to thirty pounds per square inch for clarification and evaporation, and careful cleaning to prevent fermentation. The manufacture also recovers apple seeds from the pomace, and the seeds are valuable enough to pay the daily wages of all the workers.

l: apple jelly, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_packaged_in wooden buckets [five- and ten-pound sizes for family use] Apple jelly emerges from the evaporator at about 30 to 32 degrees Baume, the consistency found suitable after cooling. It is mixed to equalize variations in concentration and flavor, then drawn hot into wooden buckets and other packages for shipment. Each bushel of fruit produces about four to five pounds of jelly; crab apples produce the finest jelly, sour natural fruit makes the best-looking article, and mixed varieties provide satisfactory flavor and quality.

l: apples, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Apple jelly is made in a factory from apples received in 500- to 1,000-bushel bins. Natural, ungrafted, crabbed, gnarled, or frozen apples may be used; frozen fruit must arrive solid. Later-ripening fruit yields more jelly, and crab apples yield the finest jelly.

l: cider, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Cider is produced by grinding and pressing the apples, then is clarified and partially concentrated before becoming jelly. It may also be exchanged to farmers for apples, sold as boiled cider, or drawn from an upper evaporator tube at a desired consistency for pies and sauces. The account states that turning cider into jelly gives it twice the value for food purposes that it has as a beverage and intoxicant.

l: apple press (apple jelly factory), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The apple press, made wholly of iron and powered by water for all motions and screw turning, presses layered apple cheese enclosed in strong cotton cloth, replacing straw and straining the cider, to produce cider.

l: defecator (apple jelly factory), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The defecator is an eleven-foot by three-foot copper pan with steam-heated copper tubes. It clarifies cider as pomace and particles rise as scum removed by a floating rake, then partially evaporates the cider to about 20 degrees Baume before it enters the evaporator.

l: evaporator (apple jelly factory), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The evaporator is a system of six twelve-foot, three-inch copper tubes, each with an iron steam jacket. Powered by boiler-furnace steam at twenty-five to thirty pounds pressure, it receives cider from the defecator through a strainer. Sirup passes through for about three minutes, increasing from 20–23 to 30–32 degrees Baume to produce apple jelly; pressure controls reduction.

l: apple jelly production (1880), Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: produced forty-five tons of apple jelly [in 1880, besides cider and boiled cider] The factory near Mexico was erected late in the season of 1880 and produced about forty-five tons of apple jelly that year. In 1880, when the apple crop was superabundant, the factory paid six to eight cents per bushel for apples.

l: apple jelly production, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Apple jelly manufacture at the Mexico factory produced 1,500 to 1,800 pounds per ten-hour day, with improvements planned for more than one ton daily. Four to five pounds came from each bushel of apples, then jelly was packaged hot for shipment.

l: improved grape bag, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The improved grape bag, invented by M. Pelletier, is a grape bag fitted with a curved glass square on a light iron-wire support. Its glass-covered sun-facing portion increases light and warmth while an air layer prevents scorching, hastening grape maturity and providing up to 10 degrees more warmth than bags alone. It protects grapes from exposure and protects sulphur from driving rain, supporting mildew control. More effective than a plain grape bag, it suits wall-grown or screened grapes and is made in varied sizes for ripening pears and other choice fruits, while helping prevent ripe fruit from falling.

l: M. Pelletier, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: has_address 20 Rue de la Banque, Paris M. Pelletier, of 20 Rue de la Banque, Paris, invented the improved grape bag. He found that curved glass was more effective than plain glass and had the bags made in varying sizes and shapes for use with different fruits.

l: grapes, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_grown_in outdoor grape cultivation [in limited varieties] The grapes discussed are difficult to ripen outdoors in the comparatively sunless and moist climate described. With careful training, stopping of laterals, mildew control, thinning, and exposure to sun and air, good edible grapes might often be produced. Glass-fronted bags are expected to improve their quality, maturity, and protection from rain and falling.

l: outdoor grape cultivation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Outdoor grape cultivation contrasts strikingly with cultivation under glass: only about two varieties commonly ripen outdoors, and they do not always succeed. Improved culture and glass-fronted bags may enable it in higher latitudes and ripen continental varieties.

l: summers, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are comparatively sunless and moist [in the climate discussed] The summers are characterized as comparatively uncertain, sunless, moist, and sometimes marked by a low average temperature. The improved grape bag is presented as a means of partly neutralizing these conditions by giving fruit additional warmth.

l: solar heat utilization apparatus, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The solar heat utilization apparatus concentrates solar rays in a reflector that tracks the sun and heats a vertical boiler, using solar heat as motive power. Made in different sizes, its portable form can be carried on a man's back, boil about two and one-half quarts an hour after thirty or forty minutes of heating, and support six or eight men with four gallons of water daily. It can provide drinking and cooking water and operate a printing machine, pump, and other equipment, though it is not yet perfected.

l: solar heat, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_obscured_by clouds [often in France] Solar heat was used to replace fuel for printing, pumping, making cider, and making coffee. In a country with uninterrupted sunshine, it could heat the apparatus's boiler in thirty or forty minutes.

l: solar rays, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_concentrated_by solar heat utilization apparatus [in a reflector] The apparatus concentrates the solar rays in a reflector that moves at the same rate as the sun. The text presents their concentrated heat as a possible source of motive power and of boiling water.

l: English public and military authorities, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: are_urged_to_attend_to solar heat utilization apparatus [immediately] They are urged to give the apparatus immediate attention because it might benefit English troops serving abroad. The writer argues that the invention is especially important to England at that time.

l: Professor Mouchon, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Professor Mouchon of Tours, a professor, originated and began constructing a solar-heat utilization apparatus about fifteen years earlier; M. Pifre later developed the idea experimentally.

l: M. Pifre, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: M. Pifre continued Professor Mouchon’s solar-heat experiments, investing substantial labor and expense; later company support enabled apparatus of varying sizes at a factory capable of larger production.

l: water, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: can_be_purified_by solar heat utilization apparatus [even when of the worst quality] The portable apparatus could provide about four gallons of water a day, enough by distillation or boiling to supply six or eight men. If water of even the worst quality was available, it could provide good drinking and cooking water.

l: soldier, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: can_use solar heat utilization apparatus [in India or Egypt and in the field] The apparatus could enable a soldier in India or Egypt to obtain good water in the field and cook food rapidly.

l: Indian troops, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: may_benefit_from solar heat utilization apparatus [in India] Indian troops might find the apparatus of inestimable value, even after the Egyptian question was settled.

l: commission, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A commission is urged to inspect solar heat apparatus at 30 Rue d'Assas, report promptly, and determine whether it is suitable for adoption.

l: How to Establish a True Meridian, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a paper [read before the Engineers' Club of Philadelphia] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] It explains how to establish a true meridian by determining latitude from an observation of Polaris and then correcting an observation at Polaris's eastern or western elongation by the star's azimuth. It also describes the equipment, observations, computations, and checks needed in practical surveying.

l: L. M. Haupt, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: authored How to Establish a True Meridian [as professor] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] L. M. Haupt, identified as a professor, wrote the unit and read it as a paper before the Engineers' Club of Philadelphia. He seeks to make the determination of a true meridian sufficiently clear and practical for general use.

l: true meridian, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A north-and-south line through the poles, established by surveying Polaris with latitude- and date-based azimuth correction, then used to determine magnetic variation, local time, and longitude differences.

l: magnetic needle, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Magnetic needle is a navigation instrument praised for guiding mariners and explorers, but is unsatisfactory for accurately determining permanent boundary lines; true-meridian traversing is recommended instead where practicable.

l: Polaris, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Polaris is a circumpolar star near the north pole, apparently revolving around the celestial poles every 23 hours 56 minutes. Its specified orbit radius and polar distance support azimuth calculations. Selected to establish a true meridian, its corrected transit altitude gives latitude and its elongation azimuth marks the meridian.

l: eastern elongation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] The eastern elongation is the point at which Polaris is farthest east of the meridian. At this position the star is moving up or down in the direction of the vertical wire, so the exact time of elongation need not be known precisely.

l: western elongation, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] The western elongation is the point at which Polaris is farthest west of the meridian. An observation at this point can be corrected by the tabulated azimuth so that the instrument is brought into the meridian.

l: latitude, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: equals altitude [the altitude of the pole at the place of observation] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] The latitude of the place is found from the corrected altitude of Polaris at upper or lower meridian transit, with the star's polar distance subtracted or added as appropriate. The text establishes that the altitude of the pole equals the latitude of the place of observation.

l: azimuth, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Azimuth is an angle between an object's vertical plane and the meridian plane, measured on the horizon from south through west and north. For Polaris, it depends on latitude and changes slightly yearly as polar distance changes.

l: altitude, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_a coordinate [distance of a celestial object above the horizon] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] Altitude is the distance of a celestial object above the horizon measured along a vertical circle. The observed altitude of Polaris must be corrected by subtracting refraction before it is used to determine latitude.

l: transit, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_used_for true meridian [with a vertical arc and horizontal wire] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] At upper or lower transit, Polaris crosses the meridian and its observed altitude can be used to determine latitude. The text warns that a small timing error at transit can produce a significant angular error because the star is then moving across the meridian.

l: surveying, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: uses true meridian [as a more accurate reference than the magnetic needle] APPROXIMATE EQUATION OF TIME.] The unit advocates determining surveying lines from a true meridian rather than relying on the magnetic needle. Practical work requires a transit with a vertical arc, lighting or reflecting equipment, plumb bobs, stakes, and related instruments.

l: azimuth table, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Azimuth table for establishing a true meridian lists Polaris azimuths by date, latitude 26–50° north, and years 1882–1886, showing azimuths increase with latitude and decrease slightly annually at a fixed point.

l: equation of time, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Equation of time is a date-and-minute table correcting observed solar time to true or mean solar time, showing when clock is faster or slower than sun; it is 4 minutes January 1, falling to 0 April 15.

l: Rheinardius ocellatus, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Rheinardius ocellatus is the type of a new genus in Phasianidae, connected after a manner with Argus and pheasants. More than two meters long, it is dominated by an extraordinary tail comprising about three-fourths of its length. Twelve broad, plane rectrices taper regularly and bear ocellated spots; the tail is held slightly elevated and its point reaches the soil. It has a small head with an erectable brown-and-white piliform occipital crest, silky brown and silvery gray head feathers, and ruddy brown neck feathers. Its blackish upper body and reddish brown underpart are spotted white or cafe-au-lait, with marked wings and remiges. The bird has a dark rose-colored argus-like beak, long spur-less legs, and delicate, partly webbed front toes.

l: Museum of Natural History of Paris, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Museum of Natural History of Paris, formerly holding only caudal feathers of unknown origin, received from Mr. Maingonnat a magnificent, perfectly adult Rheinardius ocellatus specimen.

l: Argus, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Argus is the genus after which Rheinardius ocellatus is placed in the Phasianidae. Rheinardius ocellatus is described as connecting Argus, in a manner, with the pheasants properly so-called.

l: Phasianidae, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Rheinardius ocellatus is placed in the family Phasianidae. The bird is distinguished from other phasianids described in the text by its exceptionally long, broad tail, its occipital tuft, and its particular coloration.

l: Tonkin, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: contains Buih-Dinh [locality of capture; 400 kilometers south of Hue] A specimen of Rheinardius ocellatus was captured in a portion of Tonkin that was still unexplored by Europeans. The locality was named Buih-Dinh, 400 kilometers south of Hue.

l: Borneo, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: is_inhabited_by Argus [common Argus of Borneo] The common Argus of Borneo is contrasted with Rheinardius ocellatus. Unlike that bird, Rheinardius ocellatus does not have excessively elongated secondaries or a tail with two very long, roof-like feathers.

l: adult specimen of Rheinardius ocellatus, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: A perfectly adult, magnificently preserved specimen called “THE OCELLATED PHEASANT” was captured in unexplored Tonkin and given to the Museum of Natural History of Paris by Mr. Maingonnat. Its tail feathers exactly matched museum feathers; it was neither peacock nor ordinary Argus of Malacca.

l: capture of Rheinardius ocellatus, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: occurred_in Buih-Dinh [locality in Tonkin, 400 kilometers south of Hue] The capture of Rheinardius ocellatus took place at Buih-Dinh, in a part of Tonkin not yet explored by Europeans. The captured bird was subsequently given to the Museum of Natural History by Mr. Maingonnat.

l: Maidenhair tree, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Maidenhair tree is an ornamental deciduous tree with long-stalked, fan-shaped leaves that turn pale yellow before falling. Male catkins and female reproductive structures occur on separate plants, followed by drupaceous fruit. At Broadlands it reaches about 40 feet, with a 7-foot trunk girth and 45-foot spread.

l: Gingkgo biloba, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: Gingkgo biloba is a conifer, closely allied to the Yew, and presently the sole living representative of its genus. It existed during the coal period and tertiary epoch; related fossil forms were widespread in the northern hemisphere, while its truly wild state is unknown. Known to Kaempfer in 1690 and described in 1712, it reached France from England in the middle eighteenth century. Separate male and female plants bear catkins or flowers, then drupaceous fruit and seeds with embryos; germination produces fleshy cotyledons and leaves in threes.

s: Conifers include the Maidenhair tree, which is closely allied to the Yew despite being destitute of resin. Their affinities with higher Cryptogams are illustrated by features such as the corpuscles in their seeds and the Maidenhair tree's peculiar venation.

l: The Woods of America collection, Scientific American Supplement No. 360, November 25, 1882
s: The Woods of America is a collection of American woods prepared by the American Museum of Natural History for exhibition. It contains 394 logs representing all but 26 varieties of trees indigenous to the United States, with accompanying foliage, fruits, flowers, commercial products, water-color drawings, scientific diagrams, and a herbarium. Prepared on the third floor of the Arsenal in Central Park, it is expected to be the country’s only complete collection of its kind, with no comparable royal-museum collection known in England, France, or Germany. It supports education, landscape gardening, and forest-tree conservation.
